title: Ordinals, Cardinals, and Transfinite Recursion: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The finite von Neumann ordinals, and $\omega$ as the least limit ordinal
items.statement: With $0=\varnothing$ and $\sigma(n)=n\cup\{n\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and the ordinals of [[def-ordinal]]: (i) $0,1,2,3$ are ordinals, $1=\{0\}$, $2=\{0,1\}$, $3=\{0,1,2\}=2\cup\{2\}=2^{+}$, and for each $k\le 3$ the set $k$ is exactly the set of ordinals below $k$, so $k=\{\xi:\xi<k\}$; (ii) $\omega=\mathbb{N}$ is an ordinal, $\omega$ is a limit ordinal, $\omega=\bigcup\omega$, and every element of $\omega$ is $0$ or a successor, so no element of $\omega$ is a limit ordinal; (iii) $\omega$ is the least limit ordinal: $\omega\le\gamma$ for every limit ordinal $\gamma$ ([[def-limit-ordinal]], [[lem-omega-least-limit-ordinal]]). No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For (i), expand the four sets and check the definition of an ordinal directly: each element of $k$ is a subset of $k$ for $k\le3$ (transitivity), and membership on $k$ is irreflexive, transitive, trichotomous and has a least element in every nonempty subset, because membership is the usual order on the natural numbers ([[lem-omega-least-limit-ordinal]] claim (i)) and a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{N}$ has a least element (claim (i) plus [[lem-nat-transitive-irreflexive]] for the elements). Identify $3=2\cup\{2\}=2^{+}$. For (ii) and (iii), cite claims (ii)-(iv) of [[lem-omega-least-limit-ordinal]]: $\omega$ is an ordinal, it is a limit ordinal, every $\alpha\in\omega$ is $0$ or a successor, and $\omega\le\gamma$ for every limit ordinal. The identity $\omega=\bigcup\omega$ is then the union characterisation in [[def-limit-ordinal]] applied at $\alpha=\omega$ (a nonzero ordinal is a limit ordinal if and only if $\alpha=\bigcup\alpha$), together with $\bigcup\omega\subseteq\omega$ from transitivity. No step selects from a family of sets.

items.title: A set of ordinals that is not an ordinal: $\{0,1,\omega\}$
items.statement: **FALSE.** Every set of ordinals ([[def-ordinal]]) is itself an ordinal, since membership well-orders any such set. Witness: $A=\{0,1,\omega\}$ is a set whose members are ordinals and on which $\in$ is a strict well-order, but $A$ is not transitive: $2\in\omega\in A$ while $2\notin A$, so $A$ is not an ordinal.
items.strategy:
First check that membership restricted to $A$ is a strict well-order: irreflexivity is [[lem-ordinal-basics]] claim (b), transitivity of the relation on $A$ is immediate for the only two-step chain $0\in1\in\omega$ together with $0\in\omega$, trichotomy is [[lem-ordinal-trichotomy]], and every nonempty subset of $A$ has an $\in$-least element by the second part of [[lem-ordinal-trichotomy]], a set of ordinals being well ordered by membership. Then check transitivity of the set $A$: $\omega$ is an ordinal ([[lem-omega-least-limit-ordinal]]), $2\in\omega$ because $2$ is a natural number, but $2
otin A$ since $2
e0$, $2
e1$ and $2
e\omega$ (the last because $\omega$ is a limit ordinal while $2$ is a successor, [[def-limit-ordinal]]). Hence $A$ is not transitive and therefore not an ordinal; the two clauses of [[def-ordinal]] are genuinely independent, and the well-ordering clause alone does not suffice.

items.title: Lexicographic orders: $\{0,1\}\times\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$
items.statement: Order pairs of natural numbers lexicographically: $(m,n)\prec(m',n')$ if and only if $m<m'$, or $m=m'$ and $n<n'$. Then (i) $W=\{0,1\}\times\mathbb{N}$ is well ordered by $\prec$, its initial segment below $(1,0)$ is exactly $\{0\}\times\mathbb{N}$, and $n\mapsto(0,n)$ is an order isomorphism $(\mathbb{N},<)\to(W_{<(1,0)},\prec)$; consequently $\mathbb{N}$ is order isomorphic to a proper initial segment of $W$ and not to $W$, by the mutual exclusivity in [[lem-well-order-comparability]], the unique witness being $(1,0)$; (ii) $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ is well ordered by $\prec$; (iii) if $F$ is the collapsing isomorphism of [[thm-mostowski-collapse]] for $W$, then $F(0,n)=n$ for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $F(1,0)=\omega$, so the order type of $W$ is an ordinal to which $\omega$ belongs. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For (i), let $S\subseteq W$ be nonempty; if $S$ meets $\{0\}\times\mathbb{N}$ let $n_0$ be the least $n$ with $(0,n)\in S$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), and $(0,n_0)$ is the least element of $S$ because every $(0,n)\prec(1,k)$; otherwise $S\subseteq\{1\}\times\mathbb{N}$ and the same argument in the second coordinate applies. Every element below $(1,0)$ is of the form $(0,n)$, and $(0,n)\prec(0,m)\iff n<m$, so $n\mapsto(0,n)$ is an order isomorphism onto $W_{<(1,0)}$; this is the alternative (ii) of [[lem-well-order-comparability]] for the pair $(\mathbb{N},<)$, $W$, with witness $(1,0)$, and mutual exclusivity rules out an isomorphism $\mathbb{N}\to W$. For (ii), given nonempty $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ let $m$ be the least first coordinate occurring in $S$ and then $k$ the least $n$ with $(m,n)\in S$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]); no member of $S$ has first coordinate below $m$ and none with first coordinate $m$ has second coordinate below $k$, so $(m,k)$ is the $\prec$-least member of $S$. For (iii), the recursion $F(x)=\{F(y):y\prec x\}$ gives $F(0,n)=n$ by induction on $n$ (the predecessors of $(0,n)$ are exactly the $(0,j)$ with $j<n$, [[def-initial-segment]]), hence $F(1,0)=\{F(0,n):n\in\mathbb{N}\}=\omega$ by the defining equation and the identification of $\mathbb{N}$ with $\omega$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]); since $\mathrm{ot}(W)=\{F(x):x\in W\}$ ([[thm-mostowski-collapse]]), $\omega$ is a member of the order type of $W$.

items.title: The one-point extension of a well-order, and $\omega$ with a new top element
items.statement: Let $(V,<)$ be a well-order and let $\infty\notin V$; put $W=V\cup\{\infty\}$ and define $x\prec y$ if and only if $x,y\in V$ and $x<y$, or $x\in V$ and $y=\infty$. Then (i) $W$ is a well-order, $W_{<\infty}=V$, and $V$ is order isomorphic to the proper initial segment $W_{<\infty}$, so in [[lem-well-order-comparability]] applied to $(V,<)$ and $(W,\prec)$ it is alternative (ii) that holds, with the unique witness $b=\infty$; (ii) for $V=\mathbb{N}=\omega$ the extension is equinumerous with $\omega$ ([[def-equinumerous]]) but is not order isomorphic to $(\omega,<)$: the extension has a greatest element and $\omega$ does not; (iii) the collapsing map of [[thm-mostowski-collapse]] carries this extension of $\omega$ to an order isomorphism onto the ordinal $\omega^{+}=\omega\cup\{\omega\}$, so its order type is $\omega^{+}$. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: For (i), let $S\subseteq W$ be nonempty: if $S$ meets $V$ then the least element of $S\cap V$ is the $\prec$-least element of $S$, since every member of $V$ precedes $\infty$; otherwise $S=\{\infty\}$. Every member of $V$ is below $\infty$ and no other element is, so $W_{<\infty}=V$, and the identity is an order isomorphism $V\to W_{<\infty}$; the alternatives of [[lem-well-order-comparability]] are mutually exclusive, so alternative (i) fails and the witness in (ii) is unique. For (ii) with $V=\omega$, the map sending $\infty$ to $0$ and $n$ to $\sigma(n)$ is a bijection $W\to\omega$, because $\sigma$ is injective and its image is exactly the nonzero natural numbers ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]], [[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); so $W\approx\omega$. An order isomorphism preserves the property of being a greatest element, and $\infty$ is greatest in $W$, while $\omega$ has no greatest element, since $n<\sigma(n)\in\omega$ for every $n$. For (iii), the collapse satisfies $F(n)=n$ for $n\in\omega$ by induction, hence $F(\infty)=\{F(n):n\in\omega\}=\omega$, and $\mathrm{ot}(W)=\{F(x):x\in W\}=\omega\cup\{\omega\}=\omega^{+}$, an ordinal by [[lem-ordinal-basics]] claim (c).

items.title: The lexicographic order on $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ is not a well-order
items.statement: **FALSE.** The lexicographic order $\prec$ on $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$, defined by $(a,b)\prec(c,d)$ if and only if $a<c$, or $a=c$ and $b<d$ ([[def-int-order]]), is a well-order ([[def-well-order]]). It is a total order, being the lexicographic order of two total orders, but the nonempty subset $\{0\}\times\mathbb{Z}$ has no $\prec$-least element: for every integer $n$ the element $(0,n-1)$ is already in the subset and satisfies $(0,n-1)\prec(0,n)$. So this total order is not a well-order.
items.strategy:
Totality: for distinct pairs $(a,b)
e(c,d)$, either $a
e c$ and the total order of $\mathbb{Z}$ decides, or $a=c$ and $b
e d$ and the total order of $\mathbb{Z}$ decides ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]). Then exhibit the nonempty subset $\{0\}	imes\mathbb{Z}$: for each $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ the integer $n-1$ exists in $\mathbb{Z}$ (closure under subtraction, [[thm-int-comm-ring]]) with $n-1<n$ and $0=0$, so $(0,n-1)\prec(0,n)$ lies in the subset and is strictly below $(0,n)$; hence no member is least, the subset has no least element, and [[def-well-order]] fails. The same argument shows the lexicographic order on any product one of whose factors is not well ordered fails to be a well-order, by the same one-column witness.

items.title: An explicit well-ordering of the integers: $0\prec1\prec-1\prec2\prec-2\prec\cdots$
items.statement: On $\mathbb{Z}$ define $a\prec b$ if and only if $|a|<|b|$, or $|a|=|b|$, $a\ne b$ and $0<a$ ([[def-abs-value]], [[def-int-order]]); explicitly $0\prec1\prec-1\prec2\prec-2\prec\cdots$. Then $\prec$ is a well-order of $\mathbb{Z}$: every nonempty $S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ has a $\prec$-least element, namely the unique $s\in S$ attaining the least element of $\{|s|:s\in S\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ with the positive one preferred, and the initial segment below $0$ is empty; for $a\ne0$ the initial segment below $a$ consists of $0$ and of every $\pm n$ with $1\le n<|a|$ together with $-a$ when $a<0$. The usual order of $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a well-order, so this is a different well-order of the same set; the order is given by an explicit formula and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
The relation is a strict total order: it compares the naturals $|a|$ first, with the tie $|a|=|b|$, $a
e b$ settled by putting the positive element first, and both keys are decided by the linear order of $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-nat-order]], [[thm-nat-linear-order]]; [[lem-int-abs-properties]]). For the least-element property let $S
e\emptyset$; the set $M=\{|s|:s\in S\}$ is a nonempty subset of $\mathbb{N}$ and has a least element $m$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]). If $m=0$ then $0\in S$, and $0$ is least because every other member has positive absolute value. If $m>0$ then some $s\in S$ has $|s|=m$, and $|s|=m$ means $s=m$ or $s=-m$ ([[lem-int-abs-properties]]); if $m\in S$ then $m\prec s$ for every other $s\in S$, since $|s|\ge m$ and $|s|=m$, $s
e m$ forces $s=-m$; otherwise $-m\in S$ and the same argument shows $-m$ is $\prec$-least. Because all members of $S$ have $|s|\ge m$, no member is missed. The initial segments are computed from [[def-initial-segment]] and the definition of $\prec$: $W_{<0}=\varnothing$, $W_{<1}=\{0\}$, $W_{<-1}=\{0,1\}$, $W_{<2}=\{0,1,-1\}$, and for $a
e0$ in general $W_{<a}=\{0\}\cup\{\pm n:1\le n<|a|\}$, with $-a$ added when $a<0$. The relation is given by one explicit formula on $\mathbb{Z}$, so nothing is selected.

items.title: The shift $x\mapsto x+1$ is a nonidentity order automorphism of $(\mathbb{Z},<)$
items.statement: **FALSE.** Each of claims (a) and (c) of [[lem-well-order-rigid]] holds for every total order, i.e. totality in place of well-ordering suffices. Witness: on $\mathbb{Z}$ with its usual order ([[def-int-order]]) the shift $\sigma(x)=x+1$ is an order isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-order-isomorphism]]) with $\sigma(x)\ne x$ for every $x$, so the identity is not the only order automorphism; and $x\mapsto x-1$ is strictly increasing while $x-1<x$ for every $x$, so a strictly increasing self-map need not satisfy $a\le f(a)$.
items.strategy: Verify the counterexample directly. The map $\sigma(x)=x+1$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}$ with inverse $x\mapsto x-1$, and it preserves and reflects the order: $x<y$ if and only if $x+1<y+1$, since $x+1<y+1\iff0<y-x$ ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]], [[def-int-order]]); so $\sigma$ is an order isomorphism onto $\mathbb{Z}$ by [[def-order-isomorphism]] and it is not the identity because $\sigma(0)=1\ne0$. Likewise $x\mapsto x-1$ is strictly increasing and moves every point down, so claim (a) of [[lem-well-order-rigid]] fails for this total order. The proof of claim (a) uses the least-element property once, on $\{a:f(a)<a\}$; $\mathbb{Z}$ has no least element and the set of downward-moved points has no minimal member, which is exactly where the well-order hypothesis enters.

items.title: The Mostowski collapse of a finite chain computes its order type
items.statement: Let $W=\{a,b,c,d\}$ carry the well-order $d\prec a\prec b\prec c$ ([[def-well-order]]). The collapsing map $F(x)=\{F(y):y\prec x\}$ of [[thm-mostowski-collapse]] then has $F(d)=\varnothing=0$, $F(a)=\{0\}=1$, $F(b)=\{0,1\}=2$ and $F(c)=\{0,1,2\}=3$, so $F$ is the order isomorphism of $W$ onto the ordinal $4=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and the order type of $W$ is $4$. Any function $F'$ on $W$ with $F'(x)=\{F'(y):y\prec x\}$ for all $x\in W$ equals $F$, by the uniqueness in [[thm-mostowski-collapse]].
items.strategy: Compute the four values in order $d,a,b,c$ using the defining equation and $W_{<d}=\varnothing$, $W_{<a}=\{d\}$, $W_{<b}=\{d,a\}$, $W_{<c}=\{d,a,b\}$ ([[def-initial-segment]]): each value is the set of previous values, and the finite von Neumann numerals are $0=\varnothing$, $1=\{0\}$, $2=\{0,1\}$ and $3=\{0,1,2\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), all ordinals by [[lem-ordinal-basics]] claim (c) applied twice from $0$. The image of $F$ is $4=\{0,1,2,3\}$, an ordinal, and $x\prec y\iff F(x)\in F(y)$ holds by the computation, so $F$ is an order isomorphism onto $4$; uniqueness is the uniqueness clause of [[thm-mostowski-collapse]], which does not require inspecting another isomorphism.

references.title: A. Marks, Set Theory (Berkeley lecture notes, 2026)
references.locator: Section 4, Lemma 4.15 and Definition 4.16 (every wellordering is isomorphic to a unique ordinal) and Exercise 4.12

items.title: The collapsing recursion has no solution on $(\mathbb{Z},<)$
items.statement: **FALSE.** The recursive equation $F(a)=\{F(b):b<a\}$ has a solution for every total order, so the theorem schema [[thm-transfinite-recursion]] and its corollary [[thm-mostowski-collapse]] need only a linear order. Witness: on $(\mathbb{Z},<)$ ([[def-int-order]]) there is no function $F$ with $F(a)=\{F(b):b<a\}$ for every $a\in\mathbb{Z}$; so the least-element hypothesis cannot be weakened to totality. In ZF with Foundation ([[def-axiom-of-foundation]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-replacement]]) the equation is inconsistent, and the failure is exactly the infinite descending sequence $-1>-2>-3>\cdots$.
items.strategy: Argue by contradiction. Suppose $F$ satisfies $F(a)=\{F(b):b<a\}$ for every integer $a$; then for $a<b$ one has $F(a)\in\{F(b'):b'<b\}=F(b)$. The composition $n\mapsto F(-(n+1))$ is a class function of $n$ on $\omega$ (using the embedding of the naturals in $\mathbb{Z}$ and additive inverses, [[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[thm-int-ordered-ring]]), so Replacement applied to it makes $S=\{F(-(n+1)):n\in\omega\}$ a set. Writing $x_n=F(-(n+1))$ we have $x_{n+1}\in x_n$ for every $n$. $S$ is nonempty, so Foundation applied to $S$, a set, produces $x\in S$ with $x\cap S=\varnothing$; writing $x=x_m$ we get $x_{m+1}\in x_m\cap S$, a contradiction. Hence no such $F$ exists: with only totality, the recursion has no solution, while [[thm-mostowski-collapse]] supplies one for every well-order precisely because the least element of each complementary set is used to run the recursion on a set and not on a proper class. The argument uses only Foundation, Replacement and the integer order; no choice principle is used.

items.title: The Hartogs number of a finite set is its successor ordinal
items.statement: Let $A\approx n$ for some natural number $n$ ([[def-equinumerous]], [[def-natural-numbers]]). Then the Hartogs number $\aleph(A)$ of [[thm-hartogs]] equals $n^{+}=n\cup\{n\}=\{0,1,\dots,n\}$: the set of order types of well-orders of subsets of $A$ is exactly the set of ordinals $\alpha$ with $\alpha\le n$, and $n^{+}$ is the least ordinal that does not inject into $A$. In particular the cardinality of $A$ determines its Hartogs number, and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy: First show $\aleph(A)=\{\alpha:\alpha\ \text{injects into}\ A\}$. If $\alpha=\mathrm{ot}(S,R)$ for $S\subseteq A$ then the order isomorphism $\alpha\to S$ is an injection, giving $\alpha\preceq A$ ([[thm-hartogs]], [[thm-mostowski-collapse]]); conversely, given an injection $j:\alpha\to A$, put $S=j[\alpha]$ and $R=\{(j(\xi),j(\eta)):\xi\in\eta\}$, so that $j$ is an order isomorphism $(\alpha,\in)\to(S,R)$, $R$ well-orders $S$ and $\mathrm{ot}(S,R)=\alpha$ by uniqueness of order type. So $\aleph(A)=\{\alpha:\alpha\preceq A\}=\{\alpha:\alpha\preceq n\}$, using the bijection $A\to n$ to transport injections. Next, $\alpha\preceq n$ if and only if $\alpha\le n$: the inclusion $\alpha\subseteq n$ gives the backward direction ([[lem-ordinal-basics]] claim (f)); for the forward direction suppose $n\in\alpha$; then $n\subseteq\alpha$ by transitivity, so $n\preceq\alpha$, and with $\alpha\preceq n$ Schroeder-Bernstein ([[thm-schroder-bernstein]]) gives $n\approx\alpha$. If $\alpha\ge\omega$ then $\omega\preceq\alpha\preceq n$ and $n\preceq\omega$ give $\omega\approx n$, contradicting [[lem-pigeonhole]] claim 4; if $\alpha<\omega$ then $\alpha$ is a natural number and claim 3 forces $\alpha=n$. Hence $\alpha\le n$ in both cases. Therefore $\aleph(A)=\{\alpha:\alpha\le n\}=\{0,1,\dots,n\}=n^{+}$, and $n^{+}$ indeed does not inject into $A$, consistent with the defining property of $\aleph(A)$ in [[thm-hartogs]].

items.title: The Hartogs number of $\omega$ is a limit ordinal above $\omega$
items.statement: Let $H=\aleph(\omega)$ be the least ordinal that admits no injection into $\omega$ ([[thm-hartogs]]). Then $H$ is a limit ordinal ([[def-limit-ordinal]]) with $\omega\in H$, so $\omega<H$ and $H$ is uncountable ([[def-countable]]); explicitly $H=\{\alpha:\alpha\ \text{is at most countable}\}$ is the set of countable ordinals, and $H$ is not the successor of any ordinal. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: As in the finite case, $\aleph(\omega)=\{\alpha:\alpha\preceq\omega\}$, because an injection $\alpha\to\omega$ transports membership to a well-order of its image with order type $\alpha$ and conversely an order type anti-embeds into $\omega$ ([[thm-hartogs]], [[thm-mostowski-collapse]]). An ordinal $\alpha$ satisfies $\alpha\preceq\omega$ exactly when it is at most countable: every subset of $\omega$ is at most countable ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]) and an at most countable set embeds in $\omega$, while conversely $\alpha\preceq\omega$ presents $\alpha$ as equinumerous with a subset of $\omega$. The identity embeds $\omega$ into $\omega$, so $\omega\in H$ and $H\ne0$. $H$ is not a successor: if $H=\alpha^{+}$ then $\alpha\in H$, so there is an injection $j:\alpha\to\omega$, and the map extending $j$ by $\alpha\mapsto0$ and $\beta\mapsto\sigma(j(\beta))$ is an injection $\alpha^{+}\to\omega$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]], [[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), so $H=\alpha^{+}$ would inject into $\omega$, against the defining property of $H$. Hence $H$ is a nonzero ordinal that is not a successor, that is a limit ordinal, with $\omega\in H$. Uncountability is the defining property read against [[def-countable]].

references.title: A. Marks, Set Theory (Berkeley lecture notes, 2026)
references.locator: Section 9, Theorem 9.6 and the sentence identifying $\omega_1$ as the least uncountable ordinal; Section 10 (cofinality)

items.title: Transfinite induction fails if the least element is exempted from the hypothesis
items.statement:
**FALSE.** The hypothesis of [[thm-transfinite-induction]] may be checked only at elements other than the least element of the well-order: for a well-order $W$ with least element $m$, if $W_{<a}\subseteq S$ implies $a\in S$ for every $a
e m$, then $S=W$. Witness: $W=\omega$ with its usual order and $S=\omega\setminus\{0\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]); the implication holds at every $a
e0$ vacuously, and it fails at $a=0$, where $W_{<0}=\varnothing\subseteq S$ while $0
otin S$. Hence $S
e W$.
items.strategy:
Verify the two halves. For $a
e0$ in $\omega$ we have $0<a$, so $0\in W_{<a}$ while $0
otin S$; hence $W_{<a}\subseteq S$ is false and the implication $W_{<a}\subseteq S\Rightarrow a\in S$ holds vacuously ([[def-initial-segment]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]] gives $W_{<a}=a=\{m:m<a\}$ and $0\in a$ for $a
e0$). At $a=0$ the initial segment $W_{<0}=\varnothing$ is contained in $S$, but $0
otin S$, so the hypothesis of [[thm-transfinite-induction]] fails exactly at the least element. Therefore $S
